newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Crawling peg to raise confidence in Yugo dinar.
newsitem.headline: Crawling peg to raise confidence in Yugo dinar.

text.p: Yugoslav economists are urging the government to abandon a fixed exchange rate and launch a crawling peg mechanism and dual currency system to restore confidence in the dinar and order to the country's finances.
They also insist a change in the exchange rate mechanism can come only after economic fundamentals are restored.
Economists argue the current fixed rate of 3.3 dinar to the German mark is unsustainable in an economy running a $2 billion trade gap and huge fiscal and parafiscal deficits.

"We need the crawling peg system with precisely determined ranges and when the dinar probes those ranges the central bank would step in and intervene," Miroljub Labus of the Economics Institute told a round-table in Belgrade on Tuesday.
Labus insisted such a mechanism would help restore confidence in the dinar. "Today, nobody believes the current rate is sustainable. And the confidence is what counts in the economic policy."
Economists also agreed any attempt to launch a flexible exchange rate was premature.

After facing hyper-inflation running at 60 percent a day in 1993, the government decided to launch a new economic stabilisation programme early in 1994 and fixed the dinar to the German mark at par. In November 1995, the 70 percent devaluation pushed the dinar to 3.3.
Goran Pitic, another economist of the Economics Institute said sticking to the fixed rate means the dinar will remain overrated and will not serve to cure internal and external imbalances.
But any talks on the exchange rate mechanism are premature until the causes of inflation are eliminated, he said.
An economics professor called for urgent changes in the exchange rate policy. "The dinar rate is neither stable nor balanced," said Branislav Pelevic of the School of Economics.
Pelevic said according to the purchasing-power parity theory the real dinar rate was 54.6 percent above its current official level and would stand at five to the mark if the theory was applied.

A devaluation would bring a few benefits, but overall it was not desirable, he said. "The question is also whether a depreciation would be consistent with the export orientation proclaimed in the official 1997 economic policy paper."
Bosko Zivkovic of the CES-Mecon private economic research institute urged radical changes in the monetary system and called for an introduction of a dual currency system.

"Yugoslavia, like many other similar economies, needs a multicurrency system. Such a system increases the quantity of money in circulation but also reduces transaction costs. It would largely stabilise the finances," he said.
But he opposed abandoning the currency board mechanism, now in place, which he saw as key to overall economic stability.

Labus saw the dual currency system as a way to optimising the M1 money supply. He said M1 stood at 11.7 percent of the GDP at the end of 1994, but only at 6.7 percent one year later. At the end of 1996, M1 is seen at 6.5 percent of the GDP.
With the 1996 GDP estimated at around 80 billion dinars this percentage of M1 is not enough for the economy, he said.
"But if the central bank wanted to print money to raise M1 to 12-15 percent of the GDP, it would not increase confidence but only add to inflationary pressures."
Labus said the only alternative was to temporarily allow some hard currency to be used along with the dinar until M1 grows sufficiently to the level appropriate for the GDP.

He said this meant lower monetary sovereignty but added: "It is the only elegant way out of the situation. Now, we need more money but must not print because of lack of confidence." -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
